definition: The person who designs how a film’s title appears on the screen. The manner in which the title of a movie is displayed on the screen is widely considered an art form. Saul Bass is considered a master 'title designer.' Notable modern 'title designers' include Kyle Cooper ('Se7en,' 1995). They often collaborate with directors to establish a film’s visual identity. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted visual.
extra: Notable modern 'title designers': Kyle Cooper ('Se7en'). Often collaborate with directors to establish a film’s visual identity. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted visual.

definition: The mood or atmosphere of a film scene, often revealed by the director in how a film is directed and expressed to the audience. Examples include 'dark,' 'comedic,' 'hopeful,' or 'suspenseful.' 'Tone' shapes audience interpretation alongside 'theme' and 'style.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and directors.
extra: Examples: dark, comedic, hopeful, suspenseful. 'Tone' shapes audience interpretation alongside 'theme' and 'style.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted film.

definition: A term that means to star in or be 'billed' above the title of a film. The 'topliner' is the star of a particular film. An example would be ‘Tom Cruise in Top Gun: Maverick.’ 'Toplining' indicates a leading 'billing' and prominence in marketing. The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.
extra: Example: ‘Tom Cruise in Top Gun: Maverick’—Cruise is the topliner. Indicates leading billing and prominence in marketing. The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.

definition: Literally meaning 'forceful turn' in French. It usually refers to a 'lead actor’s' performance that was incredibly skillful, brilliant, notable, masterful, reflects a very high standard, and perfectly displays the actor’s ability. Examples include Daniel Day-Lewis in 'There Will Be Blood' (2007) and Meryl Streep in 'Sophie’s Choice' (1982). A 'tour de force' is not just good, but career-defining. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and is a testament to the importance of a well-cast film.
extra: Examples: Daniel Day-Lewis in 'There Will Be Blood,' Meryl Streep in 'Sophie’s Choice.' Not just good, but career-defining. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and is a testament to the importance of a well-cast film.

definition: A single component or channel of a 'soundtrack.' Examples include a 'dialogue track,' a 'music track,' or an 'effects track.' 'Tracks' are mixed together in 'post-production' for final audio. The term is a key part of the lexicon of sound mixers and is a testament to the importance of a well-recorded soundtrack.
extra: Examples: dialogue track, music track, effects track. Tracks are mixed together in post-production for final audio. The term is a key part of the lexicon of sound mixers and is a testament to the importance of a well-recorded soundtrack.

definition: A smooth shot in which the camera moves alongside (‘tracking within’) or follows the subject through space, usually with the camera mounted on a 'dolly' (on a 'dolly track'). A 'tracking shot' is often seen as a side-to-side motion (relative to the scene or the action). It is also known as a 'following shot' and is sometimes used interchangeably with 'dolly shot,' 'pull back shot' (pull-out, push-out, widen-out or push-back), 'track back' (moving away) or 'track in' (or 'push-in') (moving forward), or 'zoom shot.' Famous examples include the 'Copacabana' entrance in 'Goodfellas' (1990) and the trench run in '1917' (2019). 'Tracking shots' create immersion and fluid movement. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors.
extra: Famous examples: the Copacabana entrance in 'Goodfellas,' trench run in '1917.' Creates immersion and fluid movement. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-framed shot.

definition: A term that refers to a personal touch or embellishment by an actor, director, writer, producer, or head of department within a film that becomes their signature or calling card. Examples include Quentin Tarantino’s 'trunk shots,' Alfred Hitchcock’s cameos, and Wes Anderson’s symmetry. A 'trademark' distinguishes an artist’s style. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted genre.
extra: Examples: Tarantino’s trunk shots, Hitchcock cameos, Wes Anderson’s symmetry. Distinguishes an artist’s style. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted genre.

definition: A term that refers to the professional magazines and publications that report the daily or weekly entertainment news of the entertainment industry. Examples include 'Variety,' 'The Hollywood Reporter,' and 'Deadline.' These are known as ‘the trades’ in Hollywood jargon. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.
extra: Examples: 'Variety,' 'The Hollywood Reporter,' 'Deadline.' Known as ‘the trades’ in Hollywood jargon. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.

definition: A short publicity film, preview, or advertisement composed of short excerpts and scenes from a forthcoming film or coming attraction, usually two to three minutes long, often presented at the showing of another film. The name 'trailer' comes from the fact that they originally 'trailed' (followed) the feature. Now, a 'trailer' is one of the biggest marketing tools for films. The term is a key part of the lexicon of marketing professionals.
extra: Called ‘trailer’ because they originally trailed (followed) the feature. Now one of the biggest marketing tools for films. The term is a key part of the lexicon of marketing professionals and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted marketing campaign.

definition: Someone who conditions animals to perform various behaviors on cue. An example would be a dog 'trainer' for 'Marley & Me' (2008) or a horse 'trainer' for 'Westerns.' 'Trainers' must ensure animal safety and humane treatment. The term is a key part of the on-set workflow and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.
extra: Example: Dog trainers for 'Marley & Me,' horse trainers for 'Westerns.' Must ensure animal safety and humane treatment. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.

definition: One of several ways of moving from one shot or scene to the next. This can include 'transitional effects' or shots such as a 'cut,' 'fade,' 'dissolve,' and 'wipe.' A 'transition focus' between two scenes means the current scene goes out of focus and the next scene comes into focus. Examples include 'Star Wars'' iconic 'wipe transitions' and classic 'fades to black.' 'Transitions' are editing tools used to control pacing and 'tone.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of film editors and directors.
extra: Examples: Star Wars’ iconic wipe transitions, classic fades to black. Editing tools to control pacing and tone. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film editors and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted film.

definition: The person responsible for managing drivers and coordinating the transportation of a production’s cast, crew, and equipment from the various locations and sets used for filming. The 'transportation manager' is critical on 'location-heavy shoots' and coordinates vans, trucks, trailers, and 'talent' vehicles. They work closely with 'production management.' The term is a key part of the on-set workflow and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.
extra: Critical on location-heavy shoots. Coordinates vans, trucks, trailers, and talent vehicles. Works closely with production management. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.

definition: A shot in which foreground action is superimposed on a separately filmed background by 'optical printing' or 'digital compositing.' This was a predecessor of the modern 'green screen.' It was used in classics like 'Mary Poppins' (1964) but is now largely done with 'digital compositing.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of special effects professionals.
extra: Predecessor of modern green screen. Used in classics like 'Mary Poppins.' Now largely done with digital compositing. The term is a key part of the lexicon of special effects professionals and is a testament to the meticulous attention to detail that goes into a film shoot.

definition: A film made for the purpose of showing scenes from foreign, unfamiliar, or alluring places. 'Travelogues' were popular in early cinema, often shown before main features. Modern versions exist as documentaries or 'YouTube travel vlogs.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians.
extra: Popular in early cinema, often shown before main features. Modern versions exist as documentaries or YouTube travel vlogs. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted genre.

definition: A detailed literary summary or presentation of a film’s story (and each major scene), with action and characters described in prose form, and sometimes including bits of dialogue. It is often used to market and/or sell a film project or script. A 'treatment' is usually an abridged script that is longer than a 'synopsis' (a brief summation of a film). A completed 'treatment' is the late stage in the development of a 'screenplay' after several 'story conferences' have incorporated changes into the script. 'Treatments' are essential in the 'development pipeline' because they allow producers and studios to evaluate a story’s viability before a full screenplay is written. The term is a key part of the lexicon of screenwriters and film producers.
extra: Treatments are essential in the development pipeline because they allow producers and studios to evaluate a story’s viability before a full screenplay is written. The term is a key part of the lexicon of screenwriters and film producers and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.

definition: A group of three films that together compose a larger narrative and are related in subject or 'theme.' 'Trilogies' often allow for expansive storytelling—from 'The Godfather Trilogy' to 'The Lord of the Rings'—where each film both stands alone and builds into a larger 'arc.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and screenwriters.
extra: Trilogies often allow for expansive storytelling — from 'The Godfather Trilogy' to 'The Lord of the Rings' — where each film both stands alone and builds into a larger arc. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and screenwriters and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted narrative.

definition: A term that refers to 'talent' who can sing, dance, and act skillfully and equally well on a consistent basis. This is usually applicable to performers in the 'musicals genre.' It could also refer to a person who can act, direct, and write. In Broadway and Hollywood musicals, being a 'triple threat' is the gold standard—think Gene Kelly or Hugh Jackman, who seamlessly shift between acting, singing, and dancing. The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the importance of a well-cast film.
extra: In Broadway and Hollywood musicals, being a 'triple threat' is the gold standard — think Gene Kelly or Hugh Jackman, who seamlessly shift between acting, singing, and dancing. The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the importance of a well-cast film.

definition: When a film is 'in turnaround,' it means that a studio has decided to halt its development or production, allowing the project to be shopped to other studios or producers. This status indicates that the original studio is no longer pursuing the project, often due to budget concerns, creative differences, or market considerations. Many iconic films nearly died in 'turnaround'; 'Forrest Gump,' for example, was passed on before finding its eventual studio home. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film producers and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.
extra: Many iconic films nearly died in turnaround; Forrest Gump, for example, was passed on before finding its eventual studio home. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film producers and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.

definition: A term that also refers to the time between the 'wrap' of 'talent' or crew and the start of the next 'shoot day.' For example, ‘the union requires 12-hour turnaround.’ This labor-related 'turnaround' ensures rest and safety; breaking 'turnaround' rules can incur penalties under union regulations. The term is a key part of the on-set workflow and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.
extra: This labor-related turnaround ensures rest and safety; breaking turnaround rules can incur penalties under union regulations. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.

definition: Shooting the 'reverse angle.' This is especially common in dialogue-heavy scenes, where the camera switches perspective to show the other character’s reaction. The term is a key part of the on-set workflow and is a testament to the fast-paced nature of a film shoot.
extra: This is especially common in dialogue-heavy scenes, where the camera switches perspective to show the other character’s reaction. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the fast-paced nature of a film shoot.

definition: A term for a film that is marketed as having a surprise ending that shouldn’t be revealed (as a 'spoiler') to those who haven’t seen the picture. Audiences remember 'twist endings' in films like 'The Sixth Sense' (1999) or 'The Usual Suspects' (1995), where the 'reveal' redefines everything seen before. The term is a key part of the lexicon of screenwriters and film critics.
extra: Audiences remember 'twist endings' in films like 'The Sixth Sense' or 'The Usual Suspects,' where the 'reveal' redefines everything seen before. The term is a key part of the lexicon of screenwriters and film critics and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted narrative.

definition: A term that refers to a film with only two characters. These intimate stories—such as 'My Dinner with Andre' (1981)—often rely heavily on dialogue and performance rather than spectacle. The term is a key part of the lexicon of screenwriters and directors.
extra: These intimate stories — such as 'My Dinner with Andre' — often rely heavily on dialogue and performance rather than spectacle. The term is a key part of the lexicon of screenwriters and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted narrative.

definition: A medium or close-up camera shot of two people (often in dialogue with each other), often framed from the chest up, often used to contrast the two characters. 'Two shots' are staples of romantic comedies and 'buddy films,' visually emphasizing the dynamic between characters. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors.
extra: Two shots are staples of romantic comedies and buddy films, visually emphasizing the dynamic between characters. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-framed shot.

definition: When an actor is commonly (but unfairly) identified, associated with, or ‘stereotyped’ by a particular character role. 'Casting against type' is the reverse of 'typecasting.' For instance, Bela Lugosi was forever linked with 'Dracula'; some actors embrace 'typecasting,' while others fight against it. The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the importance of a well-cast film.
extra: For instance, Bela Lugosi was forever linked with 'Dracula'; some actors embrace 'typecasting,' while others fight against it. The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the importance of a well-cast film.

definition: A ¾-inch magnetic tape, which would originally be found on a professional cassette tape format. In recent years, it has been supplanted by new digital formats. It was a competing yet inferior tape format to both 'beta' and 'VHS.' 'U-matic tapes' were heavily used in TV production and education during the 1970s–80s before digital took over. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and editors.
extra: 'U-matic tapes' were heavily used in TV production and education during the 1970s–80s before digital took over. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and editors and is a testament to the evolution of film technology.

definition: A 'supporting' role for a major (sometimes minor) star that is officially credited (usually in the end credits), but no mention (or 'billing') is made in the film’s advertisements or the opening credits. These roles can surprise audiences, such as major actors showing up in a 'cameo' without advance marketing. The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.
extra: These roles can surprise audiences, such as major actors showing up in a cameo without advance marketing. The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.

definition: A role that a major (or minor) star plays that is not credited in the credits or in the film’s poster. Brad Pitt’s 'cameo' in 'Deadpool 2' (2018) as the Vanisher is a famous modern 'uncredited role.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.
extra: Brad Pitt’s cameo in 'Deadpool 2' as the Vanisher is a famous modern 'uncredited role.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of casting directors and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.

definition: A term that refers to an understated, neutral, and muted acting performance. This approach can be powerful when subtlety is needed—Ryan Gosling is often noted for his 'underacting style.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and actors.
extra: This approach can be powerful when subtlety is needed — Ryan Gosling is often noted for his 'underacting style.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and actors and is a testament to the importance of a well-cast film.

definition: The process of slowing down a camera’s 'frame rate.' This is achieved by shooting at a slower speed than the usual 24 'frames per second.' This results in the captured images appearing in fast motion. Classic silent comedies by Charlie Chaplin and Buster Keaton often used 'undercranking' to create exaggerated, sped-up action. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors.
extra: Classic silent comedies by Chaplin and Keaton often used 'undercranking' to create exaggerated, sped-up action. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted visual.

definition: When an image is photographed with less light than what would be considered proper exposure. This results in a dimly lit, indistinct image that lacks contrast and is the opposite of an 'overexposed shot.' 'Underexposure' can be a mistake, but filmmakers sometimes use it intentionally to create 'mood' or 'mystery.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers.
extra: Underexposure can be a mistake, but filmmakers sometimes use it intentionally to create mood or mystery. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and is a testament to the power of a well-framed shot.

definition: A low-budget, non-commercial film, usually independently made, without the traditional sources of funding or distribution. The 1960s saw a rise in 'underground cinema' with figures like Andy Warhol and Kenneth Anger leading experimental works. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and directors.
extra: The 1960s saw a rise in 'underground cinema' with figures like Andy Warhol and Kenneth Anger leading experimental works. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and directors and is a testament to the importance of a well-crafted genre.

definition: An organization that represents the best interests of a certain segment of professionals in the motion picture industry. There are 'unions' for writers, actors, directors, and most film crews. 'Unions' negotiate contracts, pursue rights, and receive recognition. Therefore, there are rules and regulations when working with 'unions.' Examples include SAG-AFTRA for actors, DGA for directors, and IATSE for crew—each with strict guidelines for productions. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.
extra: Examples include SAG-AFTRA for actors, DGA for directors, and IATSE for crew — each with strict guidelines for productions. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the business side of the film industry.

definition: A 'Unit Production Manager' (UPM) is a member of a film production crew who plays an administrative role in the production process. The 'UPM' reports to the 'line producer' on the film, who oversees production and helps decide costs related to the daily production. As a 'UPM,' you execute the 'line producer’s' plans. 'UPMs' are crucial for keeping productions on schedule and budget; they’re the logistical backbone of film sets. The term is a key part of the on-set workflow and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.
extra: UPMs are crucial for keeping productions on schedule and budget; they’re the logistical backbone of film sets. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.

definition: A member of the 'publicity department' who works on location during the production of a movie. Their duties include setting up press visits and 'electronic press kit' interviews. In addition, the 'unit publicist' assembles the biographical materials and notes about the making of the movie that are later turned into the 'movie press kit.' 'Unit publicists' are 'itinerant'—they move from production to production and are on the production payroll. They often shape the public image of a film long before release, ensuring the right 'buzz' is created during shooting. The term is a key part of the lexicon of marketing professionals.
extra: They often shape the public image of a film long before release, ensuring the right buzz is created during shooting. The term is a key part of the lexicon of marketing professionals and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted marketing campaign.

definition: A character whose perspective we follow in the story but who lacks a certain degree of credibility. These 'narrators' may lack all the information necessary to translate the story to the audience adequately, or they have a clear bias. Classics like 'Fight Club' (1999) and 'The Usual Suspects' (1995) use 'unreliable narrators' to keep audiences guessing. The term is a key part of the lexicon of screenwriters and film critics.
extra: Classics like 'Fight Club' and 'The Usual Suspects' use unreliable narrators to keep audiences guessing. The term is a key part of the lexicon of screenwriters and film critics and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted narrative.

definition: Refers to an imaginary, ideal (or mythical), perfect state or place (especially in its laws, government, social and moral conditions), often with magical healing and restorative properties. 'Cinematic utopias' often serve as either aspirational or ironic backdrops—think 'Pleasantville' (1998) or 'Tomorrowland' (2015). The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and directors.
extra: Cinematic utopias often serve as either aspirational or ironic backdrops — think 'Pleasantville' or 'Tomorrowland.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted genre.

definition: Parallel lines in a picture that are not parallel to the 'visual plane' of the picture appear to converge in one or more 'vanishing points' inside or outside the borders of the image. It is useful to analyze a 'motion still image' regarding its 'vanishing points' because they can help to determine the height of the camera and the camera angle. If a 'motion still' has only one 'vanishing point,' it is possible to draw a horizontal line across it and get the so-called ‘horizon line,’ which marks the camera’s height when the 'frame' is taken. If there is more than one 'vanishing point,' it is necessary to find two opposite 'vanishing points,' which are mostly located 'offscreen,' and draw a line from one 'vanishing point' to the other to get the 'horizon line.' Understanding 'vanishing points' is vital in 'cinematography' and 'set design,' especially when creating 'perspective-heavy shots.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and set designers.
extra: Understanding vanishing points is vital in cinematography and set design, especially when creating perspective-heavy shots. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and set designers and is a testament to the power of a well-framed shot.

definition: A 'femme fatale' character with a bad reputation, usually seductive and scheming in nature or behavior. The archetype traces back to silent cinema, where actresses like Theda Bara embodied the 'vamp' persona. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and actors.
extra: The archetype traces back to silent cinema, where actresses like Theda Bara embodied the 'vamp' persona. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and actors and is a testament to the power of a well-cast film.

definition: A 'Variac' (short for “variable AC”) is a type of electrical transformer that can be used to adjust the voltage output of an AC power source. It is commonly used in industrial and commercial applications where a variable voltage is needed for testing or for controlling the speed of motors. 'Variac' is the trademark name of a 'variable autotransformer.' This instrument limits the voltage that goes to 'tungsten lights' and dims them. They come in 1K, 2K & 5K versions. In film sets, 'Variacs' were invaluable before digital dimming tech, allowing precise control over 'practical lighting.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and lighting technicians.
extra: In film sets, Variacs were invaluable before digital dimming tech, allowing precise control over practical lighting. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and lighting technicians and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.

definition: A variety entertainment show from the stage featuring a series of short acts—songs, dancing, acrobatics, comedy skits, and animal acts. It was highly popular in America from the late 1880s to the 1920s, when it was overtaken by 'sound films' and radio. Most of the early film, radio, and TV comedians found their start on the 'vaudeville circuit.' Stars like Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, and the Marx Brothers honed their craft in 'vaudeville' before moving into film. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians.
extra: Stars like Charlie Chaplin, Buster Keaton, and the Marx Brothers honed their craft in 'vaudeville' before moving into film. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and is a testament to the history of the film industry.

definition: A common household appliance for recording and/or playing prerecorded video tapes. See also 'VHS,' 'NTSC,' and 'PAL.' The rise of the 'VCR' in the 1980s reshaped film consumption, sparking the home video revolution and rental boom. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and is a testament to the evolution of film technology.
extra: The rise of the 'VCR' in the 1980s reshaped film consumption, sparking the home video revolution and rental boom. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and is a testament to the evolution of film technology.

definition: Directional forces that lead our eyes from one point to another in a picture or a shot. There are three main different types of 'vectors:' 'Index vectors' are the most obvious type, as they take the form of something in the shot that is clearly pointing somewhere, such as a one-way sign. 'Motion vectors' are created by elements in the shot that are moving in a certain direction, such as a bus driving left to right across the shot. 'Graphic vectors' take the form of aspects in a scene with a directional element, such as skyscrapers in a city or a sidewalk cutting through the shot. Understanding 'vectors' is key in 'cinematography' and editing, as they guide viewer attention across the 'frame.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors.
extra: Understanding 'vectors' is key in cinematography and editing, as they guide viewer attention across the frame. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-framed shot.

definition: A camera technique achieved by tracking backwards while simultaneously zooming toward the subject, or vice versa. This keeps the subject at the center of the image while the surroundings stretch or contract behind them. Also known as a 'dolly zoom,' this effect was named after Alfred Hitchcock’s prominent use in 'Vertigo' (1958). Steven Spielberg famously used this in 'Jaws' (1975) when 'Brody' realizes a shark attack is happening on the beach. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors.
extra: Spielberg famously used this in 'Jaws' when 'Brody' realizes a shark attack is happening on the beach. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-framed shot.

definition: A 'video' is a film or television programme recorded digitally (or, in the past, on tape) for people to watch on a television set. Today, 'video' is used broadly, covering everything from 'streaming content' to social media clips. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the evolution of film technology.
extra: Today 'video' is used broadly, covering everything from streaming content to social media clips. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the evolution of film technology.

definition: Camera Assistants take the images generated by the film or digital cameras and display them live on 'video monitors' so the director and other crew members can see exactly what’s being shot and can also see footage being played back for review. 'Video assist' became an industry standard after Jerry Lewis pioneered its use in the 1960s for reviewing 'takes.' The term is a key part of the on-set workflow and is a testament to the fast-paced nature of a film shoot.
extra: Video assist became industry standard after Jerry Lewis pioneered its use in the 1960s for reviewing takes. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the fast-paced nature of a film shoot.

definition: The tent/area where the 'monitors' are set up for the director/s, producer/s, and 'script supervisor.' On set, this is the 'nerve center' for 'creative decision-making' during a shoot. The term is a key part of the on-set workflow and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.
extra: On set, this is the nerve center for creative decision-making during a shoot. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the importance of a well-managed film crew.

definition: A person who works in the 'video medium'—recording 'moving images' and sound onto 'linear analog' or 'digital tape,' 'non-linear digital disc,' or any other 'digital recording media,' such as 'memory cards.' Unlike 'cinematographers,' 'videographers' are often associated with events, news, or smaller-scale productions. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the evolution of film technology.
extra: Unlike cinematographers, videographers are often associated with events, news, or smaller-scale productions. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film professionals and is a testament to the evolution of film technology.

definition: A popular format for 'VCR systems' worldwide in the 1990s. The 'VHS' vs. 'Betamax' format war ended with 'VHS' dominance, cementing it as the home video standard for decades. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and is a testament to the evolution of film technology.
extra: The 'VHS' vs. 'Betamax' format war ended with 'VHS' dominance, cementing it as the home video standard for decades. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians and is a testament to the evolution of film technology.

definition: Usually a type of 'action film' in which the protagonist takes the law into his/her own hands as a self-appointed doer of 'justice,' 'revenge,' and 'payback.' Examples include 'Death Wish' (1974) and 'Taxi Driver' (1976), where societal failures push individuals toward violent justice. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and directors.
extra: Examples include 'Death Wish' and 'Taxi Driver,' where societal failures push individuals toward violent justice. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and directors and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted genre.

definition: A scene in a movie that can stand on its own. For example, the 'orgasm scene' in 'When Harry Met Sally...' (1989) is often viewed and referenced on its own, separated from the rest of the film. A 'vignette' can also refer to a 'masking device,' often with soft edges. Filmmakers like Richard Linklater often structure films around a series of 'vignettes' rather than a single 'plotline.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and screenwriters.
extra: Filmmakers like Richard Linklater often structure films around a series of 'vignettes' rather than a single plotline. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film critics and screenwriters and is a testament to the power of a well-crafted narrative.

definition: Anything added to a movie that was not in the original shot under the subcategory of 'special effects.' They can either be achieved through 'CGI' or through special techniques, such as 'rear projection' and 'double exposures.' 'VFX' today includes everything from Marvel’s 'CGI-heavy blockbusters' to subtle 'digital touch-ups.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of special effects professionals.
extra: VFX today includes everything from Marvel’s 'CGI-heavy blockbusters' to subtle digital touch-ups. The term is a key part of the lexicon of special effects professionals and is a testament to the meticulous attention to detail that goes into a film shoot.

definition: The person that prepares the 'miniature models,' 'creature puppets,' or whatever the camera subject is, to perform whatever the object is supposed to do during the shot. 'Riggers' create 'digital skeletons' for '3D computer-generated' (CG) characters. These skeletons, or 'rigs,' are like puppets that define the movements of a character or creature, such as how a big cat runs, how a person’s face and mouth move when they sing, or how someone raises an eyebrow. 'Rigging' is critical for believable animation—Pixar films, for example, rely heavily on advanced 'rigging systems.' The term is a key part of the lexicon of special effects professionals.

definition: A single shot taken with a 'lens' that has a 'variable focal length,' thereby permitting the 'cinematographer' to change the distance between the camera and the object being filmed and rapidly move from a 'wide-angle shot' to a 'telephoto shot' in one continuous movement. This camera technique makes an object in the 'frame' magnify and appear larger. The movement towards a subject to magnify it is known as 'zoom in' or 'forward zoom,' or reversed or decreased to reduce its size is known as 'zoom out/back' or 'backward zoom.' 'Zoom shots' were especially popular in 1970s cinema. Directors sometimes use them to create a sense of 'unease,' or to mimic a character’s sudden focus on something. The term is a key part of the lexicon of cinematographers and directors.

definition: An early movie process for creating 'animated projections.' Eadweard Muybridge developed the 'zoopraxiscope' in the 1870s, projecting 'sequential images of motion'—essentially a 'stepping stone' to modern cinema. The term is a key part of the lexicon of film historians.

The 'Zoptic process' was famously used for 'Superman’s flying sequences' in the 1978 film, making audiences believe Christopher Reeve was truly soaring. The term is a key part of the lexicon of special effects professionals.
